blocks.html: This suit and demand for property which the said du Tilh was making against the said Carbon Barrau his uncle (inasmuch as the matter here was criminal and capital, where the witnesses and proofs must be entire, and clearer and more shining than the sun a) gave great colour to finding good the objection which the same du Tilh had, at the confrontations, proposed against the said Carbon his uncle. And it is nothing to say that the civil law, which has rejected the testimony of one against whom we have a suit in a criminal matter, does not for that reason reprove it if the suit is brought civilly, in a civil and pecuniary matter b, as was the case between the said du Tilh and Barrau. For to this there are two answers. The first: that this ruling has no place where the objection is proposed by one accused of a crime c, especially if the crime is capital, and so the head is at stake. For besides that, as we have said above, the proofs in criminal causes must be clean, must shine clearer than the sun d, and be exempt from all suspicion e, it is both certain and reasonable that where the peril is greater, affairs must be handled more warily and with greater circumspection f. The second answer: where the suit between the parties should be for all their goods, or for the greater part, the ruling above would have no place g; because a suit so weighty (for goods are esteemed as the second blood and the life of a man h) seems to nourish and produce I know not what enmity, and no small one i; and a great enemy cannot (where it is objected against him) be a witness against his enemy k. Nay, even though the enmity should not appear, if he is ever so little suspected of it l. And the reason may easily be gathered from what Cicero has eloquently left in writing. Our ancestors, he says, did not wish to open this road to enmities, that it should be lawful for anyone to injure his enemy by his testimony; inasmuch as men are so far carried by passion in the hatred they bear to another, that they would readily advance and fabricate a thousand lies to injure him m. In which Cicero shows that he had in no wise caught the scent of the Christian Law, by which it is commanded — not, as the Scribes and Pharisees thought and taught it to be written in the old law: Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy n — but more holily, to love our enemies, bless them that curse us, do good to them that hate us, pray for them that calumniate and persecute us, that we may be children of our Father which is in heaven o,

notes.citation: Code 4.19.25 (De probationibus, last law); Code 7.62 (De appellationibus et consultationibus), l. Addictos — the constitution beginning Addictos supplicio (C. 7.62.29, Arcadius and Honorius)
notes.original: l. derniere C. de proba. l. addictos. C. de ap pellatio.
notes.gloss: C. 4.19.25 (Constantine): accusers must bring proofs "supported by competent witnesses, or by the plainest documents, or by indications beyond doubt and clearer than light" — the source of Coras's "clearer than the sun".

notes.citation: Authentica Si testis in Code 4.20 (De testibus), at the end (as printed; its place in the title unverified); Authenticum, seventh collation, title De testibus (Novel 90), c. 7 (Si vero quis dicat odiosum praesentem ad testimonium sibi constitutum … si criminalis inter eos lis movetur, non adsit … si … conventus pecuniarie, procedat quidem testatio), which is Coras's rule; the print's § Si vero dicatur answers to it rather than to c. 6 (Si vero dicatur servilis esse fortunae)
notes.original: Autentique ſi teſtis, à la fin. C. de teſti. P. ſi verò dica tur. de teſtib. col. vij.
notes.gloss: The Novel-derived rule that the testimony of one's adversary in a suit is excluded in criminal, not in civil, causes — the objection Coras answers.

notes.citation: Decretals, X 2.20 (De testibus), c. Testimonium (X 2.20.54) and the last chapter of the title (X 2.20.56)
notes.original: c. teſtimoniũ c. denier de te.

notes.citation: Code 4.19.25 and the law Addictos, cited above at {a}
notes.original: l. derniere & l. addictos. deſ ſus alleg.

notes.citation: Code 9.47.16 (De poenis, l. Qui sententiam); the law Addictos, Code De appellationibus, as at {a}
notes.original: l. qui ſenten t am. C. de pæ. l. addictos, C. de appel.
notes.gloss: C. 9.47.16: the judge is to pronounce no capital or severe sentence unless the accused is convicted by his own confession or by the concordant evidence of all who were examined, "so caught in the crime that he can scarcely himself deny it".

notes.citation: Digest 37.10.1 (De Carboniano edicto, l. 1), § Sed et si quis (D. 37.10.1.5); Liber Sextus, VI 1.6.3 (De electione, c. Ubi periculum)
notes.original: l. j P, ſed, & ſi quis. D. de Carb. edict. c. vbi periculũ de electio.
notes.gloss: Ubi periculum maius intenditur, ibi procul dubio est plenius consulendum — the opening of Gregory X's constitution on the conclave (Lyon, 1274): where the peril is greater, fuller precaution is to be taken.

notes.citation: Accursius (Accurſe), the gloss on the Authentica Si testis (C. 4.20), cited above at {b}
notes.original: Accurſe en l'Autenti. ſi te ſtis, deſſus alleguee.
l. aduocati C. de aduoc. diuer. iud.
notes.gloss: Advocates who settle the doubtful fortunes of causes "provide for mankind no less than if they saved their country and their kin by battles and wounds" — the equation of goods with life.

notes.citation: Digest 22.5.3 pr. (De testibus, l. 3 at the beginning); Decretals, X 5.1 (De accusationibus), cc. Repellatur (X 5.1.7, Repellantur), Qualiter (Qualiter et quando: X 5.1.17, or its Lateran IV reissue X 5.1.24) and Cum oporteat (X 5.1.19)
notes.original: l. iij au cõmẽcement D. de teſt. c. repellatur. qualiter. c. cum oporteat. de accuſatio
notes.gloss: D. 22.5.3 (Callistratus): the judge is to weigh each witness's standing, "whether he is an enemy of the man against whom he testifies".

notes.citation: Decretals, title De accusationibus, c. Cum P. Manconella (X 5.1.10, Alexander III): the print's P. is the priest's initial, not a paragraph sign
notes.original: c. cũ. P. Mãconella de accuſatio.
Ciceron en l'oraiſon pro-Fotcio & aux partitions.
notes.gloss: The Pro Fonteio is Cicero's attack on the hostile Gallic witnesses; the sentence Coras paraphrases, that "our ancestors" would not let an enemy's testimony hurt a man, was not located in either work and may be a free rendering; the rule itself is that of the Lex Iulia at D. 22.5.3.5 and of the title De accusationibus cited at {k}.
Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself; the "and hate thine enemy" is the Pharisees' addition reported at Matthew 5:43, as Coras says.

notes.original: S. Math. c. v. S. Luc vi.
notes.gloss: Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, pray for them that despitefully use you and persecute you, that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven.

notes.citation: Decretals, X 2.13 (De restitutione spoliatorum), c. Item cum quis (X 2.13.6)
